stops.name: Tournai, the hall of Childeric, king of the Salian Franks
stops.campa: A son is born to Childeric in the old Roman city on the Scheldt, and to Basina his queen, who left the king of Thuringia because she knew Childeric to be the strongest man in the world. On the first night she bids the king rise and look out from the hall, and he sees lions, unicorns and leopards walking; the second night bears and wolves; the third, dogs and lesser beasts tearing one another: the generations of the long-haired kings shown in order, and the lion at the head of them is this child, Clovis.

stops.name: Tournai, Saint-Brice, the tomb of Childeric
stops.campa: Childeric is laid in the earth by the church of Saint-Brice with his warhorses about him, his cloisonné sword, the crystal ball, the signet ring cut CHILDIRICI REGIS, and three hundred golden bees with garnet wings sewn to his cloak. The mound closes over the pagan splendor and sleeps eleven hundred years, until 27 May 1653, when the mason Adrien Quinquin's pick breaks the chamber and the bees swarm out of history: Chifflet engraves them for the Archduke, and Napoleon sews them onto his coronation mantle in place of the Bourbon lily.

stops.name: Tournai, Clovis raised king at fifteen
stops.campa: Childeric dies and Clovis his son reigns in his stead. He is fifteen years old. The Salian warriors lift the boy on the shield after the custom of the Franks and carry him about the assembly; the long hair of the kings falls to his shoulders, which no razor may touch while he rules. Around him the map is broken pieces: Syagrius the Roman at Soissons, Ragnachar at Cambrai, Chararic beyond, Sigibert the Lame at Cologne, Goths south of the Loire, Burgundians on the Rhône. He will gather every piece.

stops.name: Soissons, the field against Syagrius
stops.campa: In the fifth year of his reign Clovis marches on Syagrius, king of the Romans, son of Aegidius, who holds his seat at Soissons, the last island of Rome in the drowned province. With him comes his kinsman Ragnachar; Chararic stands at a distance, waiting to befriend the victor, and that waiting will be remembered. Clovis demands that a battlefield be made ready, and Syagrius does not delay nor fear to resist. The lines meet; the Roman army is crushed; Syagrius turns his back and flees swiftly to Alaric at Toulouse. Rome in Gaul is ended.

stops.name: Soissons, the division of the plunder and the vase
stops.campa: The army, still in heathen error, has despoiled the churches, and among the booty is a vase of wonderful size and beauty. The bishop sends messengers begging that at least the vase be returned, and the king answers: follow us to Soissons, where all is divided by lot. There, before the heaped plunder, he asks his warriors for the ewer above his share. The wiser consent: all we see is yours. But a foolish, envious and excitable fellow lifts his battle-axe and splits it, crying that the king shall have nothing but what the lot fairly bestows. Clovis carries the wound in silence one whole year.
stops.quote: I ask of you, brave warriors, not to refuse to grant me in addition to my share, yonder dish.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Toulouse, Syagrius surrendered in chains
stops.campa: Clovis sends word to Alaric, king of the Goths: give the Roman back, or know that the Franks will make war for the refusal. Alaric is afraid to incur the anger of the Franks on Syagrius' account, it is the fashion of the Goths to be terrified, Gregory writes, and he surrenders his guest bound to the envoys. Clovis puts him under guard, and when the kingdom of Soissons is fully his, he orders him executed in secret. The Gothic king who gave up a suppliant will himself be given up, at Vouillé, to the point of Clovis' own spear.

stops.name: Soissons, the Field of March, the axe answered
stops.campa: At the end of the year the army assembles in arms on the Field of March for the review of weapons. The king walks the ranks and comes to the man who struck the vase. No one, he says, has brought armor so ill-kept, neither spear nor sword nor axe serviceable, and he seizes the man's axe and casts it down. As the soldier bends to pick it up, the king drives his own axe into his skull, and orders the rest to depart, raising great dread of himself. It is the founding parable of Frankish kingship: what the king claims, no lot may deny.
stops.quote: This is what you did at Soissons to the vase.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: The Thuringian country, the tenth-year war (traditional seat on the Unstrut)
stops.campa: In the tenth year of his reign he makes war on the Thuringians and brings them under his dominion. The canon gives the campaign one sentence, as a smith gives one hammer-blow; behind it the host crosses the Rhine into his mother Basina's country and returns with the east made quiet. He has broken the Roman island and now the German marches; he has made many wars and gained many victories, and he is not yet thirty. The kingdoms around him begin to send embassies, and among the embassies goes one to Burgundy.

stops.name: Geneva, Clotilde found in exile
stops.campa: Gundobad of Burgundy has killed his brother Chilperic with the sword and drowned Chilperic's wife with a stone tied to her neck; of the two daughters, Chrona has taken the nun's habit, and the younger, Clotilde, lives at Geneva serving the poor and washing the feet of pilgrims. Clovis' envoys, sent often into Burgundy, find the maiden and see that she is of good bearing and wise, and learn she is of royal blood. Aurelian comes to her disguised as a beggar; kneeling as she washes his feet, he shows her the ring of the Frankish king, and she accepts it in secret.

stops.name: Soissons, the marriage of Clovis and Clotilde
stops.campa: Clovis sends to Gundobad asking Clotilde in marriage, and Gundobad, not daring to refuse, gives her over to the envoys. On the road she leaves the slow ox-cart and rides ahead on horseback, urging haste before her uncle repents of the gift. Clovis receives her with great joy and marries her at Soissons. She is the Christian princess who will not relent: from the marriage bed she begins her long siege of the king's soul, telling him that the idols he honors are nothing, wood and stone and metal, and that he should honor instead the God who made heaven and earth.

stops.name: Soissons, Ingomer dies in his white robes
stops.campa: The queen makes her firstborn ready for baptism, adorning the church with hangings and curtains, that the king who cannot be moved by persuasion might be urged by the mystery. The boy, named Ingomer, is baptized, and dies still wearing the white garments of his regeneration. The king is violently angry: had the child been dedicated to his gods, he would live. The queen does not bend. She gives thanks to the omnipotent God who judged her not wholly unworthy, that one born of her womb should be taken, in his baptismal robes, into the kingdom of God.
stops.quote: If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods he would certainly have lived; but as it is, since he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live at all.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Soissons, Chlodomer saved by the queen's prayer
stops.campa: A second son is born and named Chlodomer at his baptism, and he too falls sick. The king's bitterness speaks first: this one will die like his brother, baptized in the name of your Christ. But through the prayers of his mother, and at the Lord's command, the child becomes well. It is the first miracle granted inside the king's own house, and it is Clotilde's: the pagan king watches his son live and says nothing, and the queen does not cease urging him to know the true God and to leave the idols that can help neither themselves nor anyone.
stops.quote: It is impossible that anything else should happen to him than happened to his brother, namely, that being baptized in the name of your Christ, should die at once.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut)
